title: INITIAL VALIDATION OF THE COMPUTERIZED HEBREW VERSION OF THE MOREL EMOTIONAL NUMBING TEST (MENT) FOR DETECTING FEIGNED PTSD IN ISRAEL
abstract:
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is among the most prevalent mental health disorders in Israel. Due to significant secondary gains (e.g., financial compensation), there is a substantial risk of malingering. Performance Validity Tests (PVTs) are essential for diagnostic integrity. This study aimed to perform an initial validation of the computerized Hebrew version of the Morel Emotional Numbing Test (MENT) and examine its psychometric properties within a simulated malingering design.

Ninety participants were randomly assigned to either a Control group (n = 45), instructed to respond honestly, or a Simulation group (n = 45), instructed to feign PTSD symptoms based on a clinical vignette. All participants completed the MENT, the Structured Inventory of Malingered Symptomatology (SIMS), and the PTSD Checklist for DSM‑5 (PCL‑5). Three individuals were excluded due to incomplete data, resulting in a final sample of 87 (Control: n = 43; Simulation: n = 44). ROC curve analysis was used to determine optimal cut‑off scores.

The Hebrew MENT demonstrated excellent internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = 0.966) and significantly differentiated between honest and simulated responders (p < 0.001; Cohen’s d = 1.285). ROC analysis yielded an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.826, indicating acceptable discriminative accuracy. A cut‑off of five errors provided a sensitivity of 0.818 and a specificity of 0.767. Significant positive correlations were observed between MENT scores and both the SIMS Total (r = 0.643) and SIMS Affective (r = 0.633) scales.

Preliminary evidence suggests that the Hebrew version of the MENT is a promising and efficient screening tool for detecting symptom exaggeration in Israel. When combined with the SIMS Affective scale within a tiered diagnostic framework, it may help reduce false‑positive classifications. Further validation in clinical PTSD populations is required to confirm these findings.
